## Setup

The SDT models are new in bmm. Until the next CRAN release (planned before
the workshop) they live in a development version — install once with:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
remotes::install_github("venpopov/bmm@sdt-post-processing")
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(bmm)
library(brms)  # hypothesis() and other post-processing generics
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)
library(here)

source(here("_common.R"))  # shared workshop colors + ggplot theme
```
:::


## Data

Recognition memory data from Koen, Aly, Wang, & Yonelinas (2013), as
distributed with the MPTinR package: participants studied word lists and
judged old/new test words on a 6-point confidence scale (1 = *sure new* …
6 = *sure old*). Two between-subjects test conditions (48 participants
each): a recognition test under **full attention** (Experiment 2) and a
test given **immediately after study** (Experiment 4).

All columns are documented in the codebook: `data/README.md`. The
full-attention condition is also the example dataset in the Vuorre (2025)
tutorial in `resources/01_sdt/`, so you can read this notebook and that
paper side by side.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat <- read.csv(here("data", "sdt_recognition.csv"))
glimpse(dat)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
  ggplot(aes(new, old, color = condition)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = wk_colors[["grey"]]) +
```

## Specify: the model and its formula

Binary SDT describes each old/new decision with two parameters: the
distance between the noise and signal evidence distributions (sensitivity
$d'$) and the location of the decision boundary (criterion $c$; 0 =
unbiased, positive = conservative).

`sdt_binary()` expects one row per participant × stimulus class, with the
count of "old" responses and the number of trials:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
binary_counts <- dat |>
  summarise(
    n_old    = sum(say_old),
    n_trials = n(),
    .by = c(pid, condition, is_old)
  )
head(binary_counts, 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      pid      condition is_old n_old n_trials
1 full_01 full_attention      1    88      100
2 full_01 full_attention      0    22      100
3 full_02 full_attention      1    69      100
4 full_02 full_attention      0    26      100
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sdt_model <- sdt_binary(response = "n_old", stimulus = "is_old",
                        n_trials = "n_trials")
```
:::


The **formula addresses the model parameters by name** — this is the core
of the bmm workflow. One regression formula per parameter says how it
varies over conditions and participants:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_sdt <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    dprime    ~ 1 + condition + (1 | pid),
    criterion ~ 1 + condition + (1 | pid)
  ),
  data  = binary_counts,
  model = sdt_model
)
```
:::


With treatment coding (`full_attention` is the reference level), the four
population-level coefficients are:

| Coefficient | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `dprime_Intercept` | $d'$, full-attention condition |
| `dprime_conditionimmediate` | **difference in $d'$**, immediate − full attention |
| `criterion_Intercept` | criterion $c$, full-attention condition |
| `criterion_conditionimmediate` | **difference in $c$**, immediate − full attention |

Everything you know about R's linear formulas transfers: interactions,
multiple predictors, and `(1 | pid)` for hierarchical participant-level
parameters — but the "outcome" of each formula is a *cognitive model
parameter*, not a raw response.

### Optional: re-fit the model yourself

You do **not** need this to follow the workshop. Re-fitting requires the
Stan toolchain (`Install_Packages.R`, Part 2) and takes a few minutes:
the full fitting script is `models/fit_sdt.R`.

## Evaluate: posteriors, hypotheses, model checks

The posterior draws of the coefficients *are* draws of the SDT
parameters, so condition-specific $d'$ and $c$ are simple sums of draws:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sdt_pars <- fit_sdt |>
  spread_draws(b_dprime_Intercept, b_dprime_conditionimmediate,
               b_criterion_Intercept, b_criterion_conditionimmediate) |>
  mutate(
    dprime_full = b_dprime_Intercept,
    dprime_imm  = b_dprime_Intercept + b_dprime_conditionimmediate,
    c_full      = b_criterion_Intercept,
    c_imm       = b_criterion_Intercept + b_criterion_conditionimmediate
  )

sdt_pars |>
  pivot_longer(dprime_full:c_imm,
               names_to = c("parameter", "condition"), names_sep = "_") |>
  group_by(parameter, condition) |>
  median_qi(value)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 8
  parameter condition   value .lower  .upper .width .point .interval
  <chr>     <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>  <chr>    
1 c         full      -0.0246 -0.112  0.0575   0.95 median qi       
2 c         imm       -0.222  -0.308 -0.124    0.95 median qi       
3 dprime    full       1.45    1.32   1.57     0.95 median qi       
4 dprime    imm        1.16    1.05   1.28     0.95 median qi       
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sdt_pars |>
  pivot_longer(dprime_full:c_imm,
               names_to = c("parameter", "condition"), names_sep = "_") |>
  mutate(parameter = recode(parameter, dprime = "d'", c = "criterion c"),
         condition = recode(condition, full = "full attention", imm = "immediate")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = condition, fill = condition)) +
  stat_halfeye(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(wk_colors[c("blue", "orange")]), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Posterior value", y = NULL) +
  theme_workshop()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_sdt_files/figure-html/posterior-plot-1.png){fig-alt='Posterior distributions of d-prime and criterion for the full-attention and immediate conditions, shown as halfeye plots.' width=672}
:::
:::


### Testing parameter differences is one line

Because condition differences are *coefficients on the parameters*,
testing them needs no extra machinery:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Does sensitivity differ between the two test conditions?
hypothesis(fit_sdt, "dprime_conditionimmediate = 0")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Hypothesis Tests for class b:
                Hypothesis Estimate Est.Error CI.Lower CI.Upper Evid.Ratio
1 (dprime_condition... = 0    -0.29      0.09    -0.46    -0.11         NA
  Post.Prob Star
1        NA    *
---
'CI': 90%-CI for one-sided and 95%-CI for two-sided hypotheses.
'*': For one-sided hypotheses, the posterior probability exceeds 95%;
for two-sided hypotheses, the value tested against lies outside the 95%-CI.
Posterior probabilities of point hypotheses assume equal prior probabilities.
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Is the immediate group more liberal (lower criterion)?
hypothesis(fit_sdt, "criterion_conditionimmediate < 0")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Hypothesis Tests for class b:
                Hypothesis Estimate Est.Error CI.Lower CI.Upper Evid.Ratio
1 (criterion_condit... < 0    -0.19      0.06    -0.29    -0.09        999
  Post.Prob Star
1         1    *
---
'CI': 90%-CI for one-sided and 95%-CI for two-sided hypotheses.
'*': For one-sided hypotheses, the posterior probability exceeds 95%;
for two-sided hypotheses, the value tested against lies outside the 95%-CI.
Posterior probabilities of point hypotheses assume equal prior probabilities.
```


:::
:::


Participants tested immediately after study show *lower* sensitivity and
a *more liberal* criterion than participants tested under full attention
after a filler task — and the model quantifies both differences with full
posterior uncertainty, from one formula.

### Model-implied ROC

The bmm SDT toolkit turns the posterior into the classic SDT graphics —
here the model-implied ROC curve with the observed operating points:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(roc_sdt(fit_sdt), observed = roc_observed(fit_sdt))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_sdt_files/figure-html/roc-1.png){fig-alt='Model-implied ROC curves with credible bands and observed operating points per condition.' width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attr(auc_sdt(fit_sdt), "summary")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   AUC_mean AUC_lower AUC_upper      condition
1 0.8465360 0.8253593 0.8659609 full_attention
2 0.7939292 0.7699698 0.8176885      immediate
```


:::
:::


And the latent-distribution view that every SDT figure in a textbook
draws by hand — reconstructed from the fitted posterior:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(latent_sdt(fit_sdt))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](01_sdt_files/figure-html/latent-1.png){fig-alt='Model-implied noise and signal evidence distributions with the estimated criterion.' width=672}
:::
:::


## Extension: rating-scale SDT

The 6-point confidence ratings contain more information than the binary
old/new split: `sdt_rating()` places $K-1 = 5$ confidence thresholds on
the same latent evidence axis. It expects one count column per rating
category:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rating_counts <- dat |>
  count(pid, condition, is_old, rating) |>
  complete(nesting(pid, condition, is_old), rating, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rating, values_from = n,
              names_prefix = "r", values_fill = 0)
head(rating_counts, 4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 9
  pid     condition      is_old    r1    r2    r3    r4    r5    r6
  <chr>   <chr>           <int> <int> <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>
1 full_01 full_attention      0    37    30    11    16     5     1
2 full_01 full_attention      1     2     7     3     6     3    79
3 full_02 full_attention      0    32    26    16     6    14     6
4 full_02 full_attention      1     6    12    13     9    16    44
```


:::
:::


Recognition ROCs are classically *asymmetric* — old items have more
variable memory strength than new items, the very phenomenon Koen et al.
(2013) studied. With rating data, bmm can estimate that signal-SD ratio
(`sdratio`) — the unequal-variance SDT model — with one more formula
line, while `dprime` and `criterion` keep their condition effects:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_rating <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    dprime    ~ 1 + condition + (1 | pid),
    criterion ~ 1 + condition + (1 | pid),
    spacing   ~ 1,
    sdratio   ~ 1
  ),
  data  = rating_counts,
  model = sdt_rating(response = paste0("r", 1:6), stimulus = "is_old")
)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_rating <- readRDS(here("models", "sdt_rating.rds"))
summary(fit_rating)
```

`exp(sdratio)` clearly above 1 (≈ 1.4) confirms the classic finding: the
old-item distribution is wider than the new-item distribution. Note a
substantive nuance: under the unequal-variance model the $d'$ difference
between conditions points the same way but is less certain — parameter
estimates depend on the measurement model, which is exactly why the model
is worth stating explicitly:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_rating |>
  spread_draws(b_dprime_conditionimmediate, b_sdratio_Intercept) |>
  mutate(sd_ratio = exp(b_sdratio_Intercept)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(b_dprime_conditionimmediate, sd_ratio)) |>
  group_by(name) |>
  median_qi(value)
```


Where to go from here: the bmm SDT article (`vignette("bmm_sdt")` in the
development version) covers the ROC/zROC diagnostics, threshold
parameterizations, and the criterion-free `sdt_mafc()` and
`sdt_ranking()` models; the Vuorre (2025) preprint in `resources/01_sdt/`
builds the same models from raw brms formulas.
